"Imminent" describes something that is about to happen very soon — so soon that it could occur at almost any moment. The key idea is time: the event hasn't happened yet, but it is right on the edge of happening, with barely any gap left.

Think of it this way: you're standing under a tree, and you see a huge branch directly above you cracking, bending, starting to give way. The branch hasn't fallen yet — but it's about to, and you have almost no time left. That falling branch is imminent.
What makes something "imminent" — the three built-in ideas

When someone calls something imminent, they are quietly saying three things at once.

First: it hasn't happened yet. Imminent always refers to the near future, not the present. If the storm is already hitting you, you wouldn't say it's imminent — you'd say it's here. Imminent = not yet, but any moment now.

Second: it is going to happen very soon. Not eventually. Not sometime next month. Soon — with a strong sense of urgency and almost no time left to prepare or react.

Third: it is highly likely or unavoidable. You wouldn't call something imminent if it's just a vague possibility. The word carries a strong sense that this will happen. It's not "might occur someday" — it's "this is coming, and fast."

Imminent almost always has a tone of urgency and tension. It signals: pay attention, act now, there is no time to waste. This is why you'll see it most often in high-stakes situations — emergencies, danger, crises, threats, warnings.

Here are natural examples of how the word is actually used:

  • "The hurricane is imminent — evacuate immediately."
  • "The patient was in imminent danger of losing consciousness."
  • "War seemed imminent as troops massed at the border."
  • "The company's collapse appeared imminent after the scandal broke."
  • "Rain is imminent — take an umbrella."

Notice that in all these cases, the event is very close in time, serious in nature, and feels almost inevitable.
Does it always signal something bad?

Mostly, yes — in practice, people tend to use "imminent" for events that are serious, threatening, or at least significant. But this is a matter of habit and convention, not a rule baked into the definition itself. Technically, you could say "victory is imminent" or "the good news is imminent," and it would be grammatically correct. In everyday usage though, you'll encounter it far more with negative or high-stakes events, because those are the situations where urgency needs to be expressed sharply.

"Imminent" is slightly formal. In casual speech, people might say "about to happen," "coming any second," or "right around the corner." But in journalism, law, medicine, and emergency contexts — anywhere that precision and seriousness matter — "imminent" is the exact, efficient word for the job.

You'll encounter it most in: news reports ("an imminent attack"), medical language ("imminent organ failure"), legal documents ("imminent threat of harm"), weather alerts ("imminent danger zone"), and military or political writing.
The most important mistake to avoid — imminent vs. eminent

This is the single most common confusion with this word, and it's worth knowing cold.

Imminent (what we've been learning) means about to happen very soon: "The deadline is imminent."

Eminent (a completely different word) means distinguished, respected, or standing out above others — it describes people or things of great prominence: "She is an eminent surgeon."

These two words look almost identical, sound nearly the same, and mean completely different things. The trick: if you're talking about time and something approaching, it's imminent (think: "incoming"). If you're talking about a person's greatness or fame, it's eminent.

There is also a third look-alike — immanent — a rare philosophical term meaning "inherent within" or "present throughout" something. You're unlikely to meet it in everyday life, but now you won't be surprised if you do.

If you can substitute the phrase "about to happen at any moment" into a sentence and it still makes sense, then "imminent" is the right word. If what you actually mean is "very important" or "highly respected," then you want a different word entirely.

"Imminent" is a precise, powerful word. It tells you that something significant is sitting right at the doorstep of the present moment — not here yet, but barely a breath away, almost certainly coming, and demanding your immediate attention. Whenever you see or hear it, think: the clock has nearly run out.
